reason: Gives an operational test (what would an attacker have to defeat: logic, a person or organisational decision, or matter). It settles the pairs that are easy to mix up: full-disk encryption (logic, so technical, even though it sits on a physical laptop), the AUP and background checks (a human or organisational decision, so administrative), and the door and fence (solid, so physical). It points away from sorting by asset, which is where I hesitated over FDE and the server-room door.

Names the specific trap, which is sorting by the protected asset: a server-room door guards computers but is physical, FDE guards a physical laptop but is technical, and an AUP guards IT but is administrative. 'Classify by the enforcer' partly overlaps hint 0, but the explicit negative rule (never by asset) adds a separate check that catches the distractors in this item set. The overlap is mild, not a restatement.

A counterfactual test, different from hint 0's 'would you owe this unhired' test. It resolves the items I hesitated on: unauthorised scan (flip: lawbreaking, so II), exaggerated pitch to a prospect (flip: deceit that applies anywhere, so II, not III), conflict of interest (flip: breaks the current engagement, so III). Two weaknesses: (a) on the 'beyond what I'm qualified for' item, the 'deceit' wording could pull it toward II if a learner reads the flip as misrepresentation instead of as undertaking work they can't do competently, although 'applies wherever you are' versus 'built into your engagement' does point it back to III; (b) for the mentoring item the flip breaks nothing (it is supererogatory), so the test gives no answer there, though nothing else competes for IV. Not strong enough for MISLEADS, but worth tightening.

Heads off the likely mistake of treating the prompt's 'unpatched server' as already identified and starting at assess. Reframing it as a vulnerability, not yet a risk, makes the learner see that asset and threat have to be named before likelihood x impact can be computed, so identify comes first.

Targets the only real hesitation in the sequence: whether residual risk is documented and accepted before or after the control goes in. 'Risk only goes down once the control works; some steps only make sense once you see what that achieved' puts apply/verify before residual documentation, and keeps choose-treatment before apply. It is a causal test, not a paraphrase.

The 'chain where each carries out the one above' test is relative, and the item set contains two policy-level statements. 'Every system must have a named owner' can easily be read as carrying out 'protect confidentiality of customer data', and as being carried out in turn by an ownership-assignment procedure, which puts it in the middle (Standard) when it is a responsibility statement (Policy). The chain also gives no position for the guideline (passphrase), which is advisory and sits beside the chain, not in it, so the hint offers no way to separate Guideline from Standard. Hint 0's binding-versus-specificity test already does this job correctly; this hint adds a test that can move the owner item to the wrong bucket.
